text.title: A/B Testing Core Rules
text.summary: 12 testable rules every A/B experiment must obey — five binding the runtime that assigns and measures, seven binding the design that is registered before it launches and the decision taken after it closes.

rule.statement: Variant assignment MUST be a deterministic function of (user_id, experiment_id, salt) via 64-bit hash mod 100. random.choice / time-based assignment / per-request RNG are forbidden.

rationale.source: Microsoft ExP guidance + Internal — A/B audits 2024

rule.rationale: Non-deterministic assignment breaks sticky bucketing; the same user gets different variants on different requests, destroying signal.

rule.statement: The bucket function MUST yield the same variant for the same user_id across web, iOS, Android, email, and server-side callbacks. Surface-local randomness is forbidden.
rule.rationale: Cross-surface variant drift produces an inconsistent user experience and biases conversion attribution.

rule.statement: Every experiment-run MUST attach an SRM check (chi-square p > 0.001 against expected split). Failed SRM invalidates the result; ship/kill decisions are blocked.

rationale.source: Kohavi et al. — Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments

rule.rationale: SRM is the canonical signal that bucketing leaked or one variant filtered users out; ignoring it produces wrong conclusions that look statistically significant.

rule.statement: Conversion events MUST only count after an exposure event has fired for the same (user_id, experiment_id). Conversions without prior exposure are dropped.
rule.rationale: Counting conversions without exposure measures the population, not the experiment; gives the false impression that the variant works on users who never saw it.

rule.statement: Decision artefact MUST report Wilson 95% CI on the conversion-rate delta, not raw percentages. A point-estimate without CI is invalid.

rationale.source: Wilson 1927 + modern stats engine output norms

rule.rationale: Raw percentages hide variance; small samples can show "10% lift" with a CI spanning -5% to +25%, i.e. no decision possible.

rule.statement: Hypothesis, primary metric, guardrail metrics and minimum detectable effect are written down and frozen BEFORE launch. Adjusting any of them after data starts arriving invalidates the experiment.

rationale.source: Kohavi, Tang, Xu — Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments

rule.rationale: Pre-registration is the only defence against moving the goalposts: with the metric chosen after the data is visible, some metric always wins, and the write-up is indistinguishable from an honest one.
rule.reference: Pre-registration plan: hypothesis, split, metrics, guardrails, sample size, timeline, risks.

rule.statement: Sample size is computed before launch from the baseline rate, the MDE, 80% power and 95% significance, and is never reduced once the experiment is running.
rule.rationale: A fixed-horizon p-value checked continuously is not a p-value. Cutting the planned sample on a positive trend inflates the false-positive rate several-fold, and the effect that looked biggest is the one most likely to be noise.
rule.reference: Sample-size calculator for the two-proportion test.

rule.statement: An experiment runs for at least one full business cycle — two weeks minimum — even when the planned sample size is reached sooner.
rule.rationale: Weekday and weekend populations behave differently, as do payday and pre-payday weeks. A three-day run that hit its sample measured whoever happened to be online on those three days, and that population is not the one the change ships to.

rule.statement: Guardrail metrics — revenue per session, error rate, latency, retention — are evaluated alongside the primary metric, and a regression on any guardrail blocks the ship regardless of how the primary metric moved.
rule.rationale: A local win that costs revenue is net-negative, and it ships anyway whenever guardrails are tracked but not gating. The gate has to be mechanical: a human reading a dashboard reliably discounts the number they did not want to see.

rule.statement: Segment analyses are named in the pre-registration. A post-hoc segment slice requires a multiple-comparison correction and is reported as exploratory, never as a result.
rule.rationale: Slice any dataset finely enough and a significant segment appears by construction. Without correction, "it won for mobile users in Germany" is a description of the noise, not of the change.

rule.statement: A statistically significant result must also clear a pre-declared practical-significance floor (e.g. +0.5 percentage points absolute) before it ships.
rule.rationale: With enough traffic every difference becomes significant. The floor is what separates a result worth the implementation and maintenance cost from one that merely cleared p < 0.05.

rule.statement: The analysis and its recommendation are advisory. A named human — PM or analyst — signs off before the ship, having reviewed the guardrails and the risk.
rule.rationale: The decision weighs organisation-specific risk tolerance and commitments that appear in no metric. An agent can compute the verdict; it cannot own the consequences of it.
